idiom_name: private_constant with an internal namespace and private methods
implementation_notes: Ruby loads source at runtime and gems are never recompiled against a header, so the firewall is about the constant and method surface: implement the body under an internal namespace and call private_constant on it (or private_class_method and private for individual methods) so external references raise NameError while the defining module still uses them, and let the file layout under lib/ decide what a consumer can require. Where a genuine opaque handle is needed it sits at the C-extension boundary, and Ruby's own TypedData API is the model: an rb_data_type_t descriptor plus TypedData_Wrap_Struct and TypedData_Get_Struct put a C struct behind a Ruby object that exposes no fields - the route Ruby core itself is taking to hide struct rb_io_t. A hand-written delegating wrapper class in pure Ruby only adds a method call per operation.
code_sketch:
# lib/ledger.rb
module Ledger
  module Impl                       # implementation namespace
    class Account
      def initialize(store) = @store = store
      def deposit(cents) = @store.append(cents)
    end
  end
  private_constant :Impl            # Ledger::Impl raises NameError from outside

  def self.account(store:) = Impl::Account.new(store)   # only this escapes
end
pitfalls: private_constant and private are receiver-enforced conventions: const_get, send and instance_variable_get walk straight through them, and any code can re-open the class and replace the body at runtime.

Gems ship their implementation, so hiding protects the API surface and versioning discipline rather than secrets; semantic versioning plus documented private markers are what actually keep consumers off internals.
At the C-extension boundary the TypedData contract is unsafe: a missing type check, dmark or dfree produces crashes and memory corruption instead of Ruby exceptions.
